title: Falmouth Stories & History
intro: Verified Falmouth history and local stories, each tied to a real place, a square on the illustrated pull-out map (letters A–F across, numbers 1–4 down, Downtown side on the front and Woods Hole side on the back), and a nearby Falmouth Wellness Discovery partner. Two East Falmouth places sit off that sheet and are marked that way. Private homes and private waterfront communities are noted so readers know what can be visited and what should only be viewed from a public way.

stories.title: Katharine Lee Bates’s birthplace
stories.summary: The author of “America the Beautiful” was born on August 12, 1859, in the Congregational parsonage at 16 Main Street, on the Village Green.
stories.body: Katharine Lee Bates was born on August 12, 1859, at 16 Main Street, then the parsonage rented by First Congregational Church for its minister, Rev. William Bates, and his family. The house itself dates to 1810. The Falmouth Historical Society bought the birthplace in 1976 and later sold it, in October 2008; it is a private residence today. Bates wrote the lines of “America the Beautiful” after a visit to Pikes Peak in 1893, taught English at Wellesley College, and is buried in Oak Grove Cemetery in Falmouth. The public places to spend time with her story are the statue on the Falmouth Public Library lawn and the collections at the library and at Falmouth Museums on the Green.
stories.visit_note: 16 Main Street is a private residence. Please view it from the sidewalk and do not approach the door.

stories.title: Katharine Lee Bates statue
stories.summary: A bronze statue of Bates, by sculptor Lloyd Lillie, stands on the lawn of Falmouth Public Library at 300 Main Street.
stories.body: A life-size bronze statue of Katharine Lee Bates stands on the lawn of Falmouth Public Library, 300 Main Street. Sculptor Lloyd Lillie portrayed her at 34, at Pikes Peak, the moment that led to “America the Beautiful.” The statue was unveiled on August 12, 1986, and dedicated on August 12, 1988, during Falmouth’s tricentennial. The library keeps a collection of her work in the Lemcke Reference Room. From the lawn it is a short walk along Main Street (Downtown D2) to the shops already in this issue.
stories.visit_note: The statue stands on the public library lawn at 300 Main Street. Check the library’s current hours if you want to see the Bates collection inside.

stories.title: Shining Sea Bikeway
stories.summary: A 10.7-mile paved rail trail from Woods Hole on Vineyard Sound to North Falmouth on Buzzards Bay, named for a line in “America the Beautiful.”
stories.body: The Shining Sea Bikeway is a 10.7-mile paved path on the old New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad bed, which carried trains between Falmouth and Woods Hole from 1872 to 1965. The town dedicated the first stretch as a bicentennial project in 1975 and extended the trail to North Falmouth in 2009. The name honors Katharine Lee Bates and the line “from sea to shining sea.” It is the only bikeway on Cape Cod that runs alongside the sea. The town maintains it for cycling, walking, jogging, skating, and cross-country skiing.
stories.visit_note: The pin marks the downtown access near Depot Avenue, a short walk from Corner Cycle on Palmer Avenue. The path continues south toward Woods Hole along Surf Drive.

stories.title: Woods Hole science and the Titanic discovery
stories.summary: WHOI, the Marine Biological Laboratory, and the nation’s oldest public marine aquarium share the Woods Hole waterfront. In 1985, a WHOI-led team helped find the wreck of RMS Titanic.
stories.body: Woods Hole, a village of Falmouth, is one of the country’s major marine-science centers. The Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI), the Marine Biological Laboratory, and NOAA’s Woods Hole Science Aquarium sit along the village waterfront. Spencer Baird established a U.S. Fish Commission research station here in 1871; a public research aquarium was added in 1875, and NOAA calls it the nation’s oldest public marine aquarium, at 166 Water Street. On September 1, 1985, a joint expedition of WHOI and France’s IFREMER, with WHOI’s Dr. Robert D. Ballard and IFREMER’s Jean-Louis Michel, found the wreck of RMS Titanic. After the French ship Le Suroît narrowed the search, WHOI’s research vessel Knorr, using the deep-towed imaging system Argo, followed a debris trail and identified a Titanic boiler. The Knorr returned to Woods Hole on September 9, 1985, to a waterfront welcome. The aquarium is the public doorway to this story — and as of November 2026 it is closed through early 2027 for foundation repairs and exhibit work.
stories.visit_note: The Woods Hole Science Aquarium at 166 Water Street is closed through early 2027 for repairs. Check NOAA’s visit page for the reopening date. WHOI and the Marine Biological Laboratory are working research campuses; enjoy the village waterfront and official visitor information rather than walking into labs.

stories.title: Nobska Light
stories.summary: The light station at Woods Hole was established in 1828; the present tower dates to 1876 and looks out over Vineyard Sound toward Martha’s Vineyard.
stories.body: Nobska Light stands at the southwestern tip of Cape Cod in Woods Hole, at 233 Nobska Road, where Buzzards Bay, Vineyard Sound, and Nantucket Sound meet, with Martha’s Vineyard and Nonamesset Island in the view. The light station was established in 1828; the present iron tower, with a brick lining, was built in 1876. It was automated in 1985 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1987. The Town of Falmouth and the Friends of Nobska Light care for the station; volunteer-led tours and a museum shop run seasonally. The Falmouth Road Race course passes the light in its first mile, and the Shining Sea Bikeway offers a winter walk in this direction (Woods Hole side B3).
stories.visit_note: The grounds are a public landmark at 233 Nobska Road, Woods Hole. Tower tours and the museum shop are seasonal — check Friends of Nobska Light for current hours before you go.

stories.title: Falmouth Road Race, start and finish
stories.summary: Since August 15, 1973, this seven-mile race has run from the Cap’n Kidd on Water Street in Woods Hole to Falmouth Heights.
stories.body: The Falmouth Road Race began on August 15, 1973, the 40th birthday of Woods Hole bartender Tommy Leonard. He organized a run from the Cap’n Kidd on Water Street in Woods Hole to Falmouth Heights, first as a fund-raiser, and the course has been a fixture of the running calendar ever since. The route is about seven miles: from Water Street over the Eel Pond drawbridge, past Nobska Light, along Surf Drive, around Falmouth Inner Harbor, and up into the Heights. In the early years the finish was at the Brothers Four, a bar across from the Casino by the Sea; both of those buildings are gone. Today runners finish at the ballfield in Falmouth Heights, between Central Park Avenue and the Falmouth Road Race Finish Line Garden.
stories.visit_note: The start is on Water Street in Woods Hole, in front of the Cap’n Kidd. The finish is the public ballfield at Central Park in Falmouth Heights. The race itself is held in August; check falmouthroadrace.com for the current date and course details.

stories.title: Highfield Hall & Gardens
stories.summary: The Beebe family’s 1878 summer mansion at 56 Highfield Drive, now a restored public hall, gardens, and arts center beside Beebe Woods.
stories.body: Highfield Hall, at 56 Highfield Drive, was built in 1878 for the Beebe family of Boston. It is one of the early summer mansions on Cape Cod and a rare surviving example of Stick-style Queen Anne architecture in the Northeast. Boston architect Carl Fehmer designed the house. The estate once included a second mansion, Tanglewood, park-like gardens, and hundreds of acres of woodland. After decades of changing owners, Tanglewood was demolished in 1977, and Highfield stood neglected until a community restoration brought it back as a public hall for art, music, and gardens. In 1972, Josephine and Josiah K. Lilly III bought the estate and gave nearly 400 acres of Beebe Woods to the town for permanent conservation. The grounds are open daily, year-round, from dawn to dusk; the hall’s gallery hours are seasonal.
stories.visit_note: The gardens and grounds at 56 Highfield Drive are open daily from dawn to dusk. The hall’s gallery hours are seasonal — check highfieldhallandgardens.org before you go.

stories.title: Falmouth Village Green, settled 1660, a town since 1686
stories.summary: English colonists settled Falmouth in 1660, and the town was incorporated in 1686. The Village Green remains the historic heart of Falmouth village.
stories.body: The Secretary of the Commonwealth records that Falmouth was settled in 1660 and incorporated as a town in 1686. The Village Green, where Main Street meets Palmer Avenue and Town Hall Square, is still the civic and historic center of Falmouth village. First Congregational Church, gathered in 1708 and moved to its present spot at 68 Main Street in 1857, looks over the Green; a Paul Revere bell in its steeple still rings. Falmouth Town Hall stands on Town Hall Square, and Falmouth Museums on the Green occupy the historic houses just up Palmer Avenue. The Green is the right place to stand when you want to feel how old the town is, then walk east down Main Street or west toward the bikeway and Highfield.
stories.visit_note: The Village Green is a public park at Main Street and Palmer Avenue, open all year. Town Hall is at 59 Town Hall Square.

stories.title: Falmouth Museums on the Green
stories.summary: The Falmouth Historical Society’s campus at 55–65 Palmer Avenue, beside the Village Green, with historic houses, a research library, and gardens.
stories.body: Falmouth Museums on the Green, the Falmouth Historical Society, occupy a campus at 55–65 Palmer Avenue, next to the Village Green. The visitor center is in Hallett Barn. The c. 1790 Dr. Francis Wicks House is the oldest house on the Town Green and is shown as a Federal-era physician’s home. The c. 1730 Conant House holds the society’s offices, exhibitions, and research library, including the exhibit “Falmouth: Changing with the Times.” The Falmouth Garden Club tends a colonial flower garden, an herb garden, and Memorial Park on the grounds. The Cultural Center, opened in 2012, hosts lectures and programs. This is the public museum for the town’s history — including the story of Katharine Lee Bates, whose nearby birthplace the society once owned.
stories.visit_note: The campus is at 55–65 Palmer Avenue. Office hours are listed as Monday–Friday, 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.; house tours and walking tours are seasonal. Call (508) 548-4857 or check museumsonthegreen.org for current hours. The gardens are open in daylight year-round.

stories.title: The Woods Hole house floats
stories.summary: A small seasonal community of house floats in Great Harbor, moored near Ram Island and Devil’s Foot Island, reached only by boat — the only community of its kind on Cape Cod.
stories.body: In Great Harbor, Woods Hole, a handful of house floats — cottages on pontoons, often called houseboats, though they have no engine of their own — form a small summer community. Town regulations allow them to be moored within 600 linear feet of Ram Island or Devil’s Foot Island in Great Harbor from mid-April to mid-November, and in Eel Pond for winter storage. The Falmouth Select Board and local reporting have described about 14 to 19 floats, and have called this the only community of its kind on Cape Cod. They can be seen from the Woods Hole waterfront; they are private seasonal homes, not a public landing.
stories.visit_note: This is a private seasonal community on the water, reached only by boat, and it is not open to visitors. Look from the public Woods Hole waterfront and Great Harbor shore; do not board, land on, or approach the floats.

stories.title: Falmouth Airpark, the fly-in neighborhood
stories.summary: Massachusetts’ only residential fly-in community, in East Falmouth off Fresh Pond Road, where homes sit along taxiways around a 2,298-foot runway.
stories.body: Falmouth Airpark (FAA identifier 5B6) is a privately owned, public-use airport and residential fly-in community in East Falmouth, reached from Fresh Pond Road north of Route 28. The Falmouth Airpark Homeowners Association is at 67 Airpark Drive. Homes are sited along grass taxiways around a 2,298-by-40-foot runway, so residents can taxi an airplane from a hangar to the strip. Flying magazine has called it the only residential airpark in Massachusetts. The airport is listed by the FAA as open to the public, with posted rules for transient aircraft; the streets around it are a private residential neighborhood, not a walking tour.
stories.visit_note: This is a privately owned airport and a residential neighborhood. Do not walk the taxiways or treat the streets as a sightseeing stop. Transient aircraft should follow current FAA and airpark rules. The community is in East Falmouth, off the illustrated pull-out map.

stories.title: Falmouth Marine Railways and the Flying Bridge
stories.summary: Founded in 1940 as Falmouth Marine Railways, the boatyard at 278 Scranton Avenue shares Falmouth Inner Harbor with the Flying Bridge Restaurant at 220 Scranton Avenue.
stories.body: Falmouth Marine & Yachting Center, at 278 Scranton Avenue on the west side of Falmouth Inner Harbor, was founded in 1940 and was originally known as Falmouth Marine Railways. The yard has served local boats for most of a century and, during World War II, work connected with the U.S. Navy. Just down the same harbor street, the Flying Bridge Restaurant occupies a waterfront building at 220 Scranton Avenue. Town assessing records list the restaurant building as dating to 1958; the Falmouth Chamber of Commerce says the restaurant was established in 1983. A claim that the restaurant dates to 1957 could not be verified, so that year is not used here. Together the railway-turned-yard and the restaurant tell the story of the inner harbor as a working and visiting waterfront.
stories.visit_note: Falmouth Marine is a working boatyard at 278 Scranton Avenue. The Flying Bridge Restaurant is next door at 220 Scranton Avenue; check the restaurant’s hours before you go. Windfall Market is farther up the same street at 77 Scranton Avenue.

stories.title: The old Casino by the Sea, Falmouth Heights
stories.summary: A Falmouth Heights landmark between the ballfield and the beach, built around 1901, rebuilt after a 1909 fire, and demolished in 2003.
stories.body: For much of the twentieth century the Casino by the Sea stood on Grand Avenue in Falmouth Heights, sandwiched between the ballfield and Falmouth Heights Beach. The original building went up around the turn of the century (local reporting has used 1901), housed a post office in its early years, burned in 1909, and was rebuilt in a Dutch Colonial style by local builder William Tobey. Over time the first floor held a movie theater, shops, and a bathhouse; in the 1920s and 1930s the second floor was the Cottage Club. In 1966 it became the Casino by the Sea nightclub and restaurant, a summer gathering place. Falmouth Road Race runners came past it just before the finish, and crowds often ended up there, though the official early finish was at the Brothers Four, across the way. The Casino was demolished on November 25, 2003. The public places that remain are the beach, the ballfield, and the race finish at Central Park.
stories.visit_note: The Casino building is gone. Stand at Falmouth Heights Beach and Central Park on Grand Avenue, Downtown side E3, to see where it stood, between the ballfield and the water.

stories.title: St. Anthony’s Church and the strawberry farmers
stories.summary: Portuguese and Cape Verdean farmers in East Falmouth helped fund St. Anthony’s Church, which opened on January 1, 1924, and became known as “the church that strawberries built.”
stories.body: In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, immigrants from the Azores, Portugal, and Cape Verde turned the sandy soil of East Falmouth into a major strawberry-growing district. Farmers along roads such as Davisville shipped berries off Cape, and for a time Falmouth was among the largest strawberry producers in Massachusetts. As early as 1919, strawberry growers began setting aside money from berries picked on a peak Sunday of the harvest — “Strawberry Sunday” — to buy land for a church where Mass could be said in Portuguese. The community appealed to the Diocese of Fall River; in 1921 Rev. Antonio M. Fortuna arrived, and St. Anthony’s Parish was formed. The church at 167 East Falmouth Highway opened on January 1, 1924, and became known as “the church that strawberries built.” In 1977 it ceased to be designated a Portuguese national church and became the parish church for the East Falmouth area, still carrying that farming story in its stained glass and memory.
stories.visit_note: St. Anthony’s Church is at 167 East Falmouth Highway, East Falmouth. It is an active parish; check falmouthcatholic.org for Mass times. The church is off the illustrated pull-out map, which covers Downtown–Main Street and Main Street & Woods Hole.
